facts.question: Where is the deepest snow in the region today, and how does it compare?

en.title: Telluride Colorado snow report: the snow depth ranking in the US West (19 November)
en.description: Telluride leads the US West with 125 cm on upper slopes on 19 November. Snow spread across the region to 782,430 km².
en.lede: Telluride holds the deepest snow in the US West right now: 125 cm (49 in) on the upper slopes as of 19 November. The mountain sits well ahead of Crested Butte at 122 cm (48 in) and Palisades Tahoe Alpine Meadows at 107 cm (42 in), making it the choice for depth-hunters across the region today.

p: Telluride shows the classic pattern of an early-season mountain: snow that builds with altitude. The base at 2,662 m has just 8 cm (3 in), mid-mountain at 3,237 m holds 40 cm (16 in), and the top at 3,812 m carries 116 cm (46 in). Most runs live in that middle band, so 40 cm is the number that matters for most skiers right now.

The region as a whole has filled in fast. Snow now covers 782,430 km² of the US West, up from 526,410 km² two days earlier. That spread reflects a system that pushed moisture across multiple states and elevations, leaving 173 of the 193 resorts in the region with snow at altitude.

sections.h: How Telluride stacks against the past
p: At mid-mountain (3,237 m), Telluride carries 56 cm (22 in) today—twice the usual depth for 19 November (30 cm / 12 in). This puts the mountain deeper than it was on this date in 30 of the last 46 winters. That is a solid early lead, not a record, but enough to open terrain that normally stays closed until December.

Crested Butte tells a different story. At the same altitude band (3,135 m), it has only 11 cm (4 in), well below the typical 31 cm (12 in) for mid-November. Only 12 of the past 46 winters on this date had snow that shallow there. Palisades Tahoe Alpine Meadows, by contrast, is running far ahead: 79 cm (31 in) at 2,243 m, deeper than every 19 November in the past 46 years; the normal is just 9 cm (4 in).

sections.h: What stations measured on the ground
p: Stations near Telluride caught heavy snow on 17 November. The Alta Lakes gauge at 3,441 m (measured 2 km away) showed 61 cm (24 in) on the ground, with 5 cm (2 in) added in 24 hours. Wolf Creek Summit at 3,331 m recorded 84 cm (33 in) on 17 November, 13 cm (5 in) of it fresh. These single-point measurements confirm that snow is real and sitting at altitude across the region.
The gap between station values and SnowScope estimates reflects the fact that stations sit in one place and catch one day's data, while the map estimates the whole upper-slope band.

sections.h: The shape of snow by height
p: Telluride's depth profile shows steep growth with elevation. From the base to the summit, snow nearly doubles every 500 m of altitude gain. The mid-mountain sits in the zone where most skiers spend their time—40 cm is enough to cover rocks and to ski for a full day without hitting ground, but thin enough that south-facing slopes may show patches of brown by afternoon.

The freezing level on 19 November ranges from 2,460 m to 3,310 m. That means wet snow below 2,460 m and dry snow above 3,310 m, with a slushy band in between. High, north-facing slopes stay the driest longest. If you are picking runs, aim for shade.

Between now and 22 November, Telluride will gain about 13 cm (5 in), split between Friday (4 cm / 2 in) and Saturday (9 cm / 4 in). That is modest, but it arrives in the forecast window, so check the map again before you book your trip. The freezing level will drop into the next few days, pushing the wet-snow line lower.

Palisades Tahoe Alpine Meadows and the Sierra resorts are forecast to pick up 26 cm (10 in) over the same three days—twice what Telluride expects. That shift keeps the Sierra in the conversation for fresh snow even as Telluride holds the depth crown today.

sections.h: What this means for your trip
p: Telluride's lead in depth is real but comes with caveats. Early-season snow is thin at the base, so focus on higher runs and avoid the bottom of trails. Rock and grass hide under shallow cover. Resorts report when they open; check Telluride's website before you drive—depth and open terrain are not the same thing.

If you are chasing the season, Palisades Tahoe Alpine Meadows is running nearly as deep (107 cm vs. 125 cm) and forecast to gain snow faster. Crested Butte lags by 3 cm—a small gap that widens if you look at the forecast. SnowScope shows the map; a probe on the mountain shows you the truth. Carry one.

advice: Ski north-facing slopes and tree areas above 3,200 m at Telluride: they hold snow longer than south-facing terrain in November.
Early-season coverage is thin. Stay on marked, groomed runs; rocks and stumps lurk under shallow snow across the base and mid-mountain.
Watch the freezing level. On 19 November it swings from 2,460 m to 3,310 m—wet snow near the base, dry snow at the peak. Expect heavy, sticky snow if you drop low.
Before you ski off-piste or tour in avalanche terrain, check the Colorado Avalanche Information Center bulletin. Telluride sits at danger level 2 today; that can change quickly with new snow.
Depth numbers are estimates. Carry a probe and test the snowpack yourself, especially on steep slopes or in gullies where snow depth varies by metres.

captions.map: Snow depth across the US West on 19 November 2026, showing Telluride leading at 125 cm on upper slopes. Palisades Tahoe Alpine Meadows and Sierra resorts carry 102–107 cm. Total snow coverage reached 782,430 km² as of this date.
